news_summary: Building strong mentorship networks boosts early-career scientists' success and enhances public trust in scientists perceived as allies.
news_summary_fr: La mise en place de solides réseaux de mentorat favorise la réussite des scientifiques en début de carrière et renforce la confiance du public envers ces scientifiques, perçus comme des alliés.
news_summary_es: La creación de redes sólidas de tutoría fomenta el éxito de los científicos que se encuentran en las primeras etapas de su carrera y refuerza la confianza del público en los científicos, a quienes se percibe como aliados.

articles.title: Successful early-career scientists rely on network of mentors
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02827-4Large networks are particularly beneficial to researchers in under-represented groups.
articles.content:
Survey finds that research mentors help junior scientists write publications and grant applications, whereas other types of mentors are helpful for landing a new job.Credit: Thomas Barwick/Getty

The most successful early-career researchers often rely on a network of mentors who each have different roles — from advising on research and grants to making professional introductions and providing emotional support, finds a study of nearly 900 scientists just starting out1.

The findings are consistent with what mentorship scholars and practitioners have long argued: no single mentor can meet all of a trainee’s scientific, professional and psychosocial needs, says Keivan Stassun, an astrophysicist at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee. “It is encouraging to see these patterns emerge so clearly in a large data set of successful early-career investigators,” says Stassun, who has won awards for his mentorship.

For the study, which was posted on the bioRxiv preprint server and hasn’t been peer-reviewed, researchers analysed responses from recipients of K awards, issued by the US National Institutes of Health for career development. These prestigious grants support early-career researchers in strengthening their research skills and provide time for training activities that prepare them to become independent investigators.

The team found that recipients had a median of 3 mentors when they applied for their awards, although some reported as many as 15. More than 90% of the awardees said that mentoring relationships resulted in publications and grants. Other common mentoring outcomes were new professional connections (88.5%) and enhanced skills (81.8%).

The authors acknowledge that although recruitment for the study targeted successful and unsuccessful award applicants, most respondents were recipients. This prevented comparisons of characteristics between those who won awards and those who didn’t, the authors write.

Different outcomes

Participants were asked to categorize their mentors into six predefined roles. All of them had a research mentor, but many others served as coaches, sponsors, connectors or peers. Connectors used their professional network to introduce the early-career researcher to useful contacts, and sponsors used their seniority and influence to advocate for their trainees and help to create opportunities. Some awardees also had an ‘identity mentor’, with whom they shared certain traits, such as gender, race, ethnicity, nationality or sexual orientation.

Different mentor roles were associated with different types of success. For instance, research mentors were most strongly associated with achievements such as writing publications, winning grants and gaining research skills. Psychosocial benefits — such as building confidence, personal growth and improved work–life balance — came from relationships with coaches, peer mentors and identity mentors. And early-career researchers were more likely to land a job because of their relationship with a connector or sponsor than through their research mentor.

This is an important takeaway, says co-author Felicia Setiono, a health-equity researcher at SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University in Brooklyn, New York. Most postdocs aspire to continue in academia, and these positions are competitive, she says. “Yet postdocs still tend to primarily rely on their main research adviser to navigate the process for pursuing their next steps,” she adds.

Under-represented scientists

Roughly 15% of awardees were from groups under-represented in science, and they in particular seem to benefit from larger mentoring networks compared with researchers outside those groups.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a study showing that diverse mentoring networks significantly benefit early-career scientists, especially those from under-represented groups, promoting equity and success in scientific careers. The findings have broad implications for improving inclusion and support in academia, which is a meaningful societal impact.
articles.personality_title: Early-career scientists succeed with diverse mentor networks
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Early-career scientists often face many challenges as they try to build their research careers. Mentors help guide them in different ways, but it has been unclear how having multiple mentors affects their success.

**What happened** – A new study looked at nearly 900 early-career researchers who received special grants from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). These grants help scientists develop their skills and become independent. The study found that most of these scientists had about three mentors, each playing different roles like research guidance, career advice, or emotional support.

**Impact** – The study showed that having a network of mentors is important because different mentors help with different goals. For example, research mentors help with writing papers and getting grants, while other mentors help with finding jobs or building confidence. Scientists from groups that are less represented in science benefited even more from having many mentors. This shows that a variety of mentor support can make a real difference in scientists’ careers.

**What's next step** – The findings suggest that early-career researchers should seek out multiple mentors to cover different needs. Universities and research programs might also encourage building diverse mentor networks to help more scientists succeed, especially those from under-represented backgrounds.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Early-career scientists are more successful when they have a network of mentors offering different kinds of support, especially those from under-represented groups.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les jeunes chercheurs réussissent grâce à un réseau diversifié de mentors
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les jeunes chercheurs rencontrent souvent de nombreux défis pour lancer leur carrière scientifique. Les mentors les guident de différentes manières, mais on ne savait pas clairement comment avoir plusieurs mentors influence leur réussite.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une nouvelle étude a examiné près de 900 jeunes chercheurs qui ont reçu des subventions spéciales des National Institutes of Health (NIH) aux États-Unis. Ces subventions aident les scientifiques à développer leurs compétences et à devenir indépendants. L’étude a révélé que la plupart avaient environ trois mentors, chacun jouant un rôle différent comme le conseil en recherche, l’aide à la carrière ou le soutien émotionnel.

**Impact** – L’étude montre que disposer d’un réseau de mentors est important parce que chaque mentor aide pour des objectifs différents. Par exemple, les mentors en recherche aident à rédiger des articles et obtenir des subventions, tandis que d’autres mentors aident à trouver un emploi ou à renforcer la confiance en soi. Les chercheurs issus de groupes sous-représentés en science ont encore plus bénéficié d’avoir plusieurs mentors. Cela montre qu’un soutien varié des mentors peut vraiment faire la différence.

**Prochaine étape** – Ces résultats suggèrent que les jeunes chercheurs devraient chercher plusieurs mentors pour couvrir différents besoins. Les universités et les programmes de recherche pourraient aussi encourager la création de réseaux de mentors diversifiés pour aider plus de scientifiques à réussir, surtout ceux issus de groupes sous-représentés.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les jeunes chercheurs réussissent mieux lorsqu’ils bénéficient d’un réseau de mentors offrant différents types de soutien, en particulier ceux issus de groupes sous-représentés.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos en inicio de carrera triunfan con redes diversas de mentores
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos que están comenzando su carrera enfrentan muchos retos para avanzar en la investigación. Los mentores los guían de distintas formas, pero no estaba claro cómo influye tener varios mentores en su éxito.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo estudio analizó a casi 900 investigadores jóvenes que recibieron becas especiales del Instituto Nacional de Salud (NIH) de Estados Unidos. Estas becas ayudan a los científicos a desarrollar habilidades y a ser independientes. El estudio encontró que la mayoría tenía unos tres mentores, cada uno con un papel distinto, como apoyo en investigación, consejos para la carrera o ayuda emocional.

**Impacto** – El estudio mostró que tener una red de mentores es importante porque cada uno ayuda con objetivos diferentes. Por ejemplo, los mentores de investigación ayudan a escribir artículos y conseguir fondos, mientras que otros ayudan a encontrar trabajo o a aumentar la confianza. Los científicos de grupos poco representados en la ciencia se beneficiaron aún más de tener varios mentores. Esto demuestra que un apoyo variado de mentores puede marcar una diferencia real.

**Próximo paso** – Los resultados sugieren que los investigadores jóvenes deben buscar varios mentores para cubrir distintas necesidades. Las universidades y programas de investigación podrían fomentar redes de mentores diversas para ayudar a más científicos a tener éxito, especialmente a los de grupos poco representados.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los científicos en inicio de carrera tienen más éxito cuando cuentan con una red de mentores que ofrecen diferentes tipos de apoyo, especialmente quienes provienen de grupos poco representados.

articles.title: People trust scientists seen to be 'on their side', UK study find
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02883-wPolitics and personal values influence people’s confidence in scientists, finds new report
articles.content:
Protesters call for the public to put stock in scientists at a UK climate march. Credit: Michael Kemp/Alamy

At a time when misinformation is rife and many seem to be questioning scientific evidence, do people really trust scientists? In the United Kingdom, the answer is mostly yes, finds a study led by the Policy Institute at King’s College London and Sense about Science, a charity based in London.

Trust in science: How to build and maintain public support in an era of polarization

Nearly two-thirds (63%) of 4,262 UK adults surveyed said they trust scientists, giving a score of 7 or higher on a zero to ten scale. Only 5% rated their trust at three or below.

To explore what drives trust and distrust of scientists, the researchers used regression modelling to identify factors most strongly associated with trust. The most influential factors were whether respondents felt that scientists are "on the side of people like them" and whether they thought of scientists as open and transparent. Both outweighed perceptions of scientific expertise.

Previous research has shown that benevolence — the idea that researchers care about society and want to do good — is a core pillar of public trust in science1. Now Bobby Duffy, director of the Policy Institute at King’s College London and one of the authors of the UK study, says that the work reveals that trust in scientists was less associated with scientists being eager to work for the good of society in general (12%) and had more to do with whether they are on the side of people like the respondent (21%).

“In a politically divided society, people become much more interested in, ‘What’s in it for me?’” says Duffy.

Where trust falters

When the researchers delved into specific fields, they found that trust declined for scientists working on vaccines, space and climate (see ‘Pockets of trust’). And more people had more confidence in academics (12%) rather than in scientists working in government (42%) and in private companies (34%). Perhaps unsurprisingly, people with little trust in scientists are more likely to think conspiracy theories about climate change, vaccines and the effects of 5G phone towers are true, says the report.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant UK study showing that a majority of people trust scientists, highlighting the importance of perceived benevolence and alignment with public values. This has broad societal implications for science communication, public policy, and combating misinformation, which are crucial for informed decision-making and democratic engagement.
articles.personality_title: Most people in UK trust scientists who seem to share their values, study finds
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the UK, many people wonder if they can trust scientists, especially with so much misinformation around. Understanding who trusts scientists and why helps improve how science is shared with the public.

**What happened** – A study by King’s College London and a charity called Sense about Science surveyed over 4,200 adults in the UK. They found that nearly two-thirds of people trust scientists, giving them a high trust score. The study showed that people trust scientists more when they feel the scientists are on their side and are open and honest. This feeling mattered more than just thinking scientists are very smart.

**Impact** – This study is important because it shows trust depends on whether people believe scientists share their values and care about them personally. For example, people trusted university scientists more than those working for the government or companies. Trust was lower for scientists in some areas like vaccines and climate. This helps explain why some people believe false ideas or conspiracy theories.

**What’s next step** – Scientists and science communicators can use this information to build stronger connections with the public by being more open and showing they care about people’s concerns. This could help reduce misinformation and make sure scientific advice is trusted and followed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – People in the UK mostly trust scientists who seem to understand and support their values, showing that trust grows from feeling personally connected, not just from expertise alone.
articles.personality_title_fr: La plupart des Britanniques font confiance aux scientifiques qui partagent leurs valeurs, selon une étude
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au Royaume-Uni, beaucoup se demandent s’ils peuvent faire confiance aux scientifiques, surtout avec la quantité de fausses informations. Comprendre qui fait confiance aux scientifiques et pourquoi aide à mieux partager la science avec le public.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une étude menée par le King’s College de Londres et l’association Sense about Science a interrogé plus de 4 200 adultes. Elle a montré que près des deux tiers des personnes font confiance aux scientifiques, leur donnant une note élevée. La confiance vient surtout du fait que les gens sentent que les scientifiques sont de leur côté et sont ouverts et honnêtes, plus que du simple fait de penser qu’ils sont très intelligents.

**Impact** – Cette étude est importante car elle montre que la confiance dépend du sentiment que les scientifiques partagent les valeurs des gens et se soucient d’eux. Par exemple, les scientifiques universitaires sont plus dignes de confiance que ceux du gouvernement ou des entreprises. La confiance est plus faible dans certains domaines comme les vaccins et le climat. Cela explique pourquoi certaines personnes croient aux fausses idées.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques et communicants peuvent utiliser ces résultats pour mieux se connecter au public en étant plus ouverts et en montrant qu’ils se préoccupent des inquiétudes des gens. Cela pourrait aider à réduire la désinformation et à faire en sorte que les conseils scientifiques soient suivis.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La plupart des Britanniques font confiance aux scientifiques qui semblent comprendre et soutenir leurs valeurs, montrant que la confiance vient surtout du lien personnel, pas seulement de l’expertise.
articles.personality_title_es: La mayoría de británicos confían en científicos que comparten sus valores, revela estudio
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el Reino Unido, muchas personas se preguntan si pueden confiar en los científicos, especialmente con tanta desinformación. Saber quién confía en los científicos y por qué ayuda a mejorar la comunicación científica.

**Qué pasó** – Un estudio del King’s College de Londres y la organización Sense about Science encuestó a más de 4,200 adultos en el Reino Unido. Encontraron que casi dos tercios confían en los científicos, dándoles una alta puntuación. La confianza depende más de sentir que los científicos están de su lado y son abiertos y honestos, que solo de pensar que son muy inteligentes.

**Impacto** – Este estudio es importante porque muestra que la confianza depende de si las personas creen que los científicos comparten sus valores y se preocupan por ellos. Por ejemplo, se confía más en científicos universitarios que en los que trabajan para el gobierno o empresas. La confianza es menor en áreas como vacunas y cambio climático. Esto ayuda a entender por qué algunas personas creen en teorías falsas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos y comunicadores pueden usar esta información para conectar mejor con el público siendo más abiertos y mostrando que les importan las preocupaciones de la gente. Esto podría ayudar a reducir la desinformación y aumentar la confianza en la ciencia.

**Conclusión en una frase** – En el Reino Unido, la mayoría confía en científicos que parecen compartir y apoyar sus valores, mostrando que la confianza crece al sentirse personalmente conectados, no solo por la experiencia.
